_sources.usda: USDA FoodData Central, https://fdc.nal.usda.gov/ (record named in each entry), read 2026-10-27
_sources.nihOds: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements fact sheets (Iron, Folate, Vitamin C, Vitamin K, Magnesium, Zinc, Potassium, Vitamin A, Calcium, Vitamin B12, Vitamin D, Vitamin E), https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/list-all/; reference intakes as listed in build_draft_batch.py (RDA for adult women)
_sources.niddk: NIDDK, Eating, Diet & Nutrition for Kidney Stones, read 2026-10-26: nuts and nut products, peanuts, rhubarb, spinach and wheat bran listed among foods to reduce for calcium oxalate stones

black-turtle-bean.desc: Beans, black turtle, mature seeds, cooked, boiled, without salt
black-turtle-bean.offers: Black turtle beans are small, dense, earthy beans. Half a cup gives about 7.7 g of protein and 7.7 g of fibre, with folate (20% of the reference), potassium and plant iron.
black-turtle-bean.how: Simmer into soups, stews and chilli, mash for burritos and tacos, or add to rice and salads. Canned beans, rinsed, are a shortcut.
black-turtle-bean.cycle: Iron needs are higher for women aged 19 to 50 (18 mg a day, against 8 mg for men), partly because of menstrual blood loss (NIH ODS). Black beans adds plant iron, which is absorbed less readily than iron from meat; vitamin C in the same meal helps.
black-turtle-bean.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
black-turtle-bean.name: Black beans

kidney-bean.desc: Beans, kidney, all types, mature seeds, cooked, boiled, without salt
kidney-bean.offers: Kidney beans are large, meaty beans with folate (about 29% of the reference in half a cup), potassium and magnesium, plus 7.7 g of protein and 5.7 g of fibre.
kidney-bean.how: Use in chilli, curries, salads and stews. Dried kidney beans must be soaked and boiled hard before eating (see the caution); canned beans are already cooked.
kidney-bean.cycle: Folate is a nutrient some women of childbearing age do not get enough of (NIH ODS); Kidney beans is a good source. No phase-specific claim is made.
kidney-bean.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
kidney-bean.reviewNote: Dried kidney beans must be boiled hard for 10 minutes (existing catalogue caution, carried over; not externally sourced).
kidney-bean.name: Kidney bean

white-beans.desc: Beans, white, mature seeds, cooked, boiled, without salt
white-beans.offers: White beans are creamy, mild beans that give potassium (about 19% of the adequate intake in half a cup), iron and magnesium, with 8.7 g of protein and 5.6 g of fibre.
white-beans.how: Simmer into soups and stews, mash into dips, or toss with olive oil, lemon and herbs for a salad.
white-beans.cycle: Iron needs are higher for women aged 19 to 50 (18 mg a day, against 8 mg for men), partly because of menstrual blood loss (NIH ODS). White beans adds plant iron, which is absorbed less readily than iron from meat; vitamin C in the same meal helps.
white-beans.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
white-beans.reviewNote: The catalogue entry "white beans" covers cannellini, navy and great northern; this is the USDA "white" record.
white-beans.name: White beans

black-eyed-pea.desc: Cowpeas, common (blackeyes, crowder, southern), mature seeds, cooked, boiled, without salt
black-eyed-pea.offers: Black-eyed peas are small, savoury beans with a lot of folate (about 44% of the reference in half a cup), plus magnesium, zinc, 6.6 g of protein and 5.6 g of fibre.
black-eyed-pea.how: Simmer with onion and spices, add to salads and grain bowls, or stew with greens.
black-eyed-pea.cycle: Folate is a nutrient some women of childbearing age do not get enough of (NIH ODS); Black-eyed peas is a good source. No phase-specific claim is made.
black-eyed-pea.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
black-eyed-pea.name: Black-eyed pea

hummus.state: prepared, commercial (contains tahini, oil and salt)
hummus.offers: Hummus is a chickpea and sesame dip. Two tablespoons give about 71 calories, a little magnesium and zinc, and some fibre, mostly from the chickpeas. It also contains oil and usually salt.
hummus.how: Spread on sandwiches and wraps, serve with vegetable sticks or pitta, or thin with lemon juice into a dressing.
hummus.cycle: No cycle-phase claim is made for hummus. As a prepared food it varies by brand, especially in salt and oil.
hummus.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
hummus.reviewNote: A prepared food that varies by brand (salt, oil, tahini); the record is the USDA commercial average.
hummus.name: Hummus

lima-bean.desc: Lima beans, large, mature seeds, cooked, boiled, without salt
lima-bean.offers: Lima beans are buttery, starchy beans with potassium (about 18% of the adequate intake in half a cup), folate and magnesium, plus 7.3 g of protein and 6.6 g of fibre.
lima-bean.how: Simmer until very tender and add to soups, succotash and stews, or mash with herbs. They must always be cooked thoroughly (see the caution).
lima-bean.cycle: Folate is a nutrient some women of childbearing age do not get enough of (NIH ODS); Lima beans is a good source. No phase-specific claim is made.
lima-bean.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
lima-bean.name: Lima bean

split-pea.desc: Peas, split, mature seeds, cooked, boiled, without salt
split-pea.offers: Split peas break down into a thick, creamy texture when cooked. Half a cup has 8.2 g of protein and 8.1 g of fibre, with folate, potassium and zinc.
split-pea.how: Simmer into soup or dal with onion and spices; they cook without soaking.
split-pea.cycle: Folate is a nutrient some women of childbearing age do not get enough of (NIH ODS); Split peas is a good source. No phase-specific claim is made.
split-pea.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
split-pea.name: Split pea

red-lentil.state: dry, uncooked (no cooked red-lentil record in USDA)
red-lentil.portion: ¼ cup dry, before cooking (USDA: 1 cup = 192 g)
red-lentil.offers: Red lentils are quick-cooking, split lentils. The figures here are for the dry lentils: a quarter cup before cooking gives 11.5 g of protein and 5.2 g of fibre, with folate, zinc and iron (20% of the reference).
red-lentil.how: Simmer for about 15–20 minutes into soups and dals, where they dissolve into a soft purée. They roughly triple in weight when cooked, so a cooked portion has about a third of these amounts.
red-lentil.cycle: Iron needs are higher for women aged 19 to 50 (18 mg a day, against 8 mg for men), partly because of menstrual blood loss (NIH ODS). Red lentils adds plant iron, which is absorbed less readily than iron from meat; vitamin C in the same meal helps.
red-lentil.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
red-lentil.reviewNote: USDA has no cooked red-lentil record, so amounts are for the DRY lentils; red lentils roughly triple in weight when cooked. The profile says so.
red-lentil.name: Red lentil

edamame.offers: Edamame are young soybeans, a plant source of complete protein: half a cup of shelled beans has 9.2 g, along with a lot of folate (about 60% of the reference), magnesium and zinc.
edamame.how: Boil or steam in the pod and squeeze the beans out, or add shelled edamame to salads, rice bowls and stir-fries.
edamame.cycle: Folate is a nutrient some women of childbearing age do not get enough of (NIH ODS); Edamame is a good source. No phase-specific claim is made.
edamame.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
edamame.name: Edamame

pinto-beans.desc: Beans, pinto, mature seeds, cooked, boiled, without salt
pinto-beans.offers: Pinto beans are mild, creamy beans with folate (about 37% of the reference in half a cup), potassium and magnesium, plus 7.7 g of protein and 7.7 g of fibre.
pinto-beans.how: Simmer for refried beans, chilli and burritos, or serve whole with rice.
pinto-beans.cycle: Folate is a nutrient some women of childbearing age do not get enough of (NIH ODS); Pinto beans is a good source. No phase-specific claim is made.
pinto-beans.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
pinto-beans.name: Pinto beans

wild-rice.offers: Wild rice is the seed of an aquatic grass, nutty and chewy. Half a cup cooked gives zinc and magnesium for about 83 calories, and more protein than most rice.
wild-rice.how: Simmer until the grains split, then use in pilafs, soups and salads, or mix with brown rice.
wild-rice.cycle: No cycle-phase claim is made for wild rice; it is a whole grain that adds zinc and magnesium to a meal.
wild-rice.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
wild-rice.name: Wild rice

farro.state: dry, uncooked, pearled (no cooked farro record in USDA)
farro.portion: 45 g dry, before cooking (USDA reference amount)
farro.offers: Farro is a chewy ancient wheat grain. The figures here are for the dry, pearled grain: 45 g before cooking gives zinc (22% of the reference), magnesium, 5.7 g of protein and 3.3 g of fibre.
farro.how: Simmer for 15–30 minutes until tender but chewy, then use in grain salads, soups and risottos. Whole farro takes longer than pearled and has more fibre.
farro.cycle: No cycle-phase claim is made for farro. It contains gluten, as it is a form of wheat.
farro.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
farro.reviewNote: USDA has only a DRY pearled farro record (Foundation); amounts are before cooking. Whole (unpearled) farro has more fibre.
farro.name: Farro

oat-bran.offers: Oat bran is the fibre-rich outer layer of the oat. Half a cup of cooked oat bran gives magnesium and some zinc and fibre for only about 44 calories.
oat-bran.how: Cook into a hot cereal with milk or water, or stir a spoonful into yoghurt, smoothies and baking.
oat-bran.cycle: No cycle-phase claim is made for oat bran. Oats can be cross-contaminated with gluten; see the caution.
oat-bran.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
oat-bran.name: Oat bran

buckwheat.offers: Buckwheat is a gluten-free seed eaten like a grain, with a toasty flavour. Half a cup of cooked roasted groats (kasha) gives magnesium and some zinc and protein.
buckwheat.how: Simmer roasted groats until tender for porridge or a side dish, or use cooled groats in salads.
buckwheat.cycle: No cycle-phase claim is made for buckwheat; it is a gluten-free whole-grain alternative.
buckwheat.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
buckwheat.name: Buckwheat (kasha)

barley.offers: Pearled barley is a chewy grain with fibre (about 3 g in half a cup), plus some zinc and iron.
barley.how: Simmer into soups and stews, cook as a risotto-style dish, or serve cooled in salads.
barley.cycle: No cycle-phase claim is made for barley. It contains gluten (see the caution).
barley.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
barley.reviewNote: Pearled barley has had part of its bran removed; hulled barley has more fibre.
barley.name: Barley

bulgur.offers: Bulgur is cracked, pre-cooked wheat. Half a cup cooked gives about 4.1 g of fibre and some magnesium and zinc for about 76 calories.
bulgur.how: Soak in hot water or simmer briefly for tabbouleh, pilafs and grain bowls.
bulgur.cycle: No cycle-phase claim is made for bulgur. It is wheat and contains gluten.
bulgur.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
bulgur.name: Bulgur

whole-grain-bread.offers: A slice of whole-wheat bread gives about 2 g of fibre with some magnesium and zinc and about 81 calories. Brands vary a lot in fibre, salt and added nutrients.
whole-grain-bread.how: Use for sandwiches and toast, or toast and top with beans, avocado or eggs.
whole-grain-bread.cycle: No cycle-phase claim is made for bread. Check the label: 'whole-wheat' is not always 'whole grain', and many breads contain added salt.
whole-grain-bread.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
whole-grain-bread.reviewNote: Commercial breads vary a lot (fibre, salt, added calcium). The record is a USDA average of whole-wheat bread, which is not necessarily whole GRAIN bread.
whole-grain-bread.name: Whole-grain bread

sesame-seeds.offers: Sesame seeds are very small, so a tablespoon is a typical serving: it gives about 88 mg of calcium and 32 mg of magnesium, with some iron and fibre.
sesame-seeds.how: Sprinkle over stir-fries, salads and rice, bake into bread, or grind into tahini. Lightly toasting brings out their flavour.
sesame-seeds.cycle: Calcium needs are 1,000 mg a day for women aged 19 to 50 (NIH ODS); a tablespoon of sesame seeds supplies about 9% of that. No phase-specific claim is made.
sesame-seeds.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
sesame-seeds.name: Sesame seeds

cashew.portion: 1 ounce (28 g), about 18 nuts (USDA: 1 oz = 28.35 g)
cashew.offers: Cashews are buttery tree nuts with magnesium (about 27% of the reference in an ounce), zinc, iron and 5.2 g of protein. They are energy dense.
cashew.how: Eat as a snack, blend soaked cashews into creamy sauces and dressings, or add to stir-fries and curries.
cashew.cycle: Iron needs are higher for women aged 19 to 50 (18 mg a day, against 8 mg for men), partly because of menstrual blood loss (NIH ODS). Cashews adds plant iron, which is absorbed less readily than iron from meat; vitamin C in the same meal helps.
cashew.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
cashew.name: Cashew

brazil-nut.offers: Brazil nuts are large, rich tree nuts. Two kernels give magnesium and some zinc and fibre for about 66 calories. They are also extremely rich in selenium, which is why only 1–2 a day is suggested.
brazil-nut.how: Eat one or two as a snack, or chop into granola or baking.
brazil-nut.cycle: No cycle-phase claim is made for Brazil nuts. The serving here is two kernels because of their selenium content.
brazil-nut.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
brazil-nut.reviewNote: The catalogue limit is 1–2 nuts a day, so the serving is 2 kernels. Brazil nuts are extremely high in selenium; selenium is not in the key list (no selenium reference was read this session) and the limit comes from the existing catalogue caution, not re-sourced here.
brazil-nut.name: Brazil nut

pecan.portion: 1 ounce (28 g), about 19 halves (USDA: 1 oz = 28.35 g)
pecan.offers: Pecans are rich, sweet tree nuts with zinc (about 16% of the reference in an ounce), magnesium and 2.7 g of fibre. They are very energy dense, at about 196 calories an ounce.
pecan.how: Eat as a snack, toast and chop over porridge or salads, or bake into cakes and pies.
pecan.cycle: No cycle-phase claim is made for pecans.
pecan.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
pecan.name: Pecan

pistachio.portion: 1 ounce (28 g), about 49 kernels (USDA: 1 oz = 28.35 g)
pistachio.offers: Pistachios are green tree nuts with potassium (about 11% of the adequate intake in an ounce), magnesium, 5.7 g of protein and 3 g of fibre.
pistachio.how: Eat shelled as a snack, chop over yoghurt and salads, or grind into pesto or baking.
pistachio.cycle: No cycle-phase claim is made for pistachios.
pistachio.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
pistachio.name: Pistachio

hazelnuts.portion: 1 ounce (28 g), about 21 kernels (USDA: 1 oz = 28.35 g)
hazelnuts.offers: Hazelnuts are sweet tree nuts that are an especially good source of vitamin E (about 28% of the reference in an ounce), with magnesium and folate.
hazelnuts.how: Eat as a snack, toast and chop over salads and desserts, or grind into nut butters and baking.
hazelnuts.cycle: No cycle-phase claim is made for hazelnuts.
hazelnuts.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
hazelnuts.name: Hazelnuts

sunflower-seeds.offers: Sunflower seed kernels are mild, nutty seeds that are exceptionally rich in vitamin E (about 82% of the reference in a quarter cup), with magnesium (about 37%), zinc, 7.3 g of protein and 3 g of fibre.
sunflower-seeds.how: Sprinkle over porridge, salads and soups, bake into bread, or blend into spreads. Toast lightly for flavour.
sunflower-seeds.cycle: No cycle-phase claim is made for sunflower seeds. A quarter cup is about 204 calories, so a spoonful or two is a more everyday amount.
sunflower-seeds.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
sunflower-seeds.name: Sunflower seeds

nut-butter.desc: Peanut butter, smooth style, without salt
nut-butter.state: smooth peanut butter, no added salt
nut-butter.offers: Two tablespoons of peanut butter give 7.1 g of protein, vitamin E (about 19% of the reference) and magnesium (about 17%). It is energy dense, at about 191 calories.
nut-butter.how: Spread on toast, stir into porridge or sauces, or blend into smoothies. Choose a type without added sugar or palm oil if you prefer.
nut-butter.cycle: No cycle-phase claim is made. This record is peanut butter; other nut butters differ.
nut-butter.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
nut-butter.reviewNote: The catalogue entry "nut butter" is generic (the existing caution says tree-nut or peanut allergen, depending on type). The record is peanut butter; almond butter and others differ.
nut-butter.name: Nut butter

mixed-nuts.desc: Nuts, mixed nuts, dry roasted, with peanuts, without salt added
mixed-nuts.state: dry roasted, with peanuts, no salt added
mixed-nuts.offers: Mixed nuts give magnesium (about 21% of the reference in an ounce), zinc, vitamin E and 5.5 g of protein, depending on the blend. They are energy dense, at about 172 calories an ounce.
mixed-nuts.how: Eat a small handful as a snack, or chop into salads, granola and baking. Unsalted blends keep the sodium down.
mixed-nuts.cycle: No cycle-phase claim is made for mixed nuts. This record is a dry-roasted mix with peanuts and no added salt.
mixed-nuts.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
mixed-nuts.reviewNote: A blend that varies by product; the record is a USDA dry-roasted mix with peanuts and no added salt.
mixed-nuts.name: Mixed nuts

peanuts.offers: Peanuts are legumes eaten like nuts. An ounce of raw peanuts gives 7.3 g of protein, folate (about 17% of the reference), vitamin E and magnesium.
peanuts.how: Eat as a snack, add to stir-fries and salads, or blend into sauces and butters.
peanuts.cycle: Folate is a nutrient some women of childbearing age do not get enough of (NIH ODS); Peanuts is a good source. No phase-specific claim is made.
peanuts.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
peanuts.name: Peanuts
